action_trace.summary: Generated 10 interview questions using 5W1H and Socratic methods to elicit user goals (passenger comfort, safety priorities), pain points (jerk-induced discomfort, conflict resolution), and acceptance criteria (curvature thresholds, obstacle handling iterations). Questions address the core conflict between SafetyAgent (passive safety) and EfficiencyAgent (smoothness/speed) while grounding requirements in measurable, lifecycle-aware trade-offs per ISO/IEC/IEEE 29148 and BABOK v3.

Generated 10 targeted interview questions using 5W1H and Socratic techniques to elicit user goals (passenger comfort, safety priority), pain points (jerk vs. safety conflicts, non-convex obstacle handling), and acceptance criteria (quantified comfort metrics, conflict resolution strategy, boundary conditions). Questions decompose the SafetyAgent/EfficiencyAgent conflict and establish operational constraints for curvature and jerk minimization in the autonomous driving case.

Generated 10 interview questions using 5W1H and Socratic techniques to elicit user goals (comfort vs. safety trade-offs), pain points (jerk sensitivity, obstacle handling, agent conflicts), and acceptance criteria (measurable comfort thresholds, priority resolution rules). Questions decompose the conflict between PassiveS Safety (curvature, MRM) and Smoothness (QP-based jerk minimization) while grounding inquiry in operating environment and user decision-making authority.

End-user pain points center on balancing passenger comfort (jerk minimization) with safety constraints (curvature, safe distances) and operational efficiency in non-convex environments. Expectations require smooth trajectory planning via QP with dynamic conflict resolution between safety and efficiency agents, supporting both highway and urban autonomous driving scenarios.

End-user perspective identifies three critical pain points: jerky motion reducing ride-sharing acceptance (jerk <0.5 m/s³ required), conservative obstacle planning increasing travel time (iterative QP needed for non-convex scenarios), and safety-efficiency conflicts creating operational bottlenecks. Expectations emphasize simultaneous achievement of passenger comfort, real-world obstacle handling, and transparent conflict resolution. Usage scenarios demonstrate requirements in urban ride-sharing and safety-critical contexts, grounding the need for integrated jerk minimization, curvature constraints, non-convex obstacle handling, and SafetyAgent-EfficiencyAgent negotiation.

End-user perspectives reveal three critical business drivers: (1) passenger comfort through jerk minimization (<0.5 m/s³) is essential for ride-sharing viability, (2) non-convex obstacle handling via iterative QP must eliminate conservative planning penalties, and (3) safety-efficiency conflict requires negotiated constraint prioritization rather than override logic. These requirements directly conflict with current SafetyAgent/EfficiencyAgent separation and demand integrated optimization framework.

Six clarification questions decompose the core conflict between safety-driven hard constraints (SafetyAgent, MRM, curvature limits) and comfort-driven optimization objectives (EfficiencyAgent, jerk minimization, speed). Key ambiguities: emergency response precedence, constraint hierarchy, real-time QP convergence requirements, scenario-specific jerk targets, and non-convex obstacle classification scope.

Nine clarification questions raised addressing: (1) priority hierarchy between safety hard constraints and jerk minimization soft constraints, (2) iterative QP real-time convergence tolerance and fallback strategies, (3) curvature constraint flexibility under varying conditions, (4) MRM execution vs. jerk continuity trade-offs, (5) obstacle complexity bounds for QP solver, and (6) passenger comfort metric validation. These questions resolve conflicts between SafetyAgent and EfficiencyAgent objectives and operationalize ambiguous requirement thresholds.

Seven clarification questions raised to resolve ambiguities in jerk minimization vs. safety prioritization, curvature constraint enforcement (hard vs. soft), iterative QP real-time convergence guarantees with acceptable suboptimality thresholds, explicit agent conflict resolution hierarchy, and dynamic vs. static curvature limit definitions. Questions ground conflict resolution in quantified metrics (time budgets, tolerance percentages, jerk thresholds) and scenario-dependent decision rules.

End-user requirements validated and refined through Chain-of-Thought analysis. Confirmed: jerk minimization <0.5 m/s³ for passenger comfort, non-convex obstacle handling via iterative QP within 100-200ms cycles. Refined: safety constraints are hard limits with absolute priority; curvature limits are vehicle-specific non-negotiable bounds; QP suboptimality tolerance is 5-10%; explicit conflict resolution hierarchy established favoring safety over smoothness and speed.

End-user confirms jerk minimization (<0.5 m/s³) and curvature constraints (κ vehicle-specific hard limits) as primary passenger comfort requirements. Refines SafetyAgent priority over EfficiencyAgent in safety-critical scenarios with temporary jerk suspension. Validates iterative QP convergence within 100-200ms with 5-10% suboptimality tolerance for real-world non-convex obstacles. All three pain points (jerky motion, conservative path planning, conflicting objectives) are now resolved through explicit priority rules and operational mode separation.

End-user confirms core requirements: jerk minimization <0.5 m/s³ for passenger comfort, vehicle-specific curvature constraints as hard limits, and iterative QP for non-convex obstacles within real-time cycles. SafetyAgent prioritized over EfficiencyAgent in safety-critical events. Requires clarification on agent mode-switching logic and QP convergence guarantees.

Consolidated 8 structured elicitation records from EndUser dialogue addressing autonomous vehicle trajectory planning. Key requirements: jerk minimization (<0.5 m/s³) for passenger comfort, vehicle-specific curvature constraints as hard safety boundaries, iterative QP for non-convex obstacles (100–200 ms convergence, 5–10% suboptimality tolerance), and explicit SafetyAgent priority over EfficiencyAgent in critical scenarios. All records follow ISO/IEC/IEEE 29148 format with source traceability, priority levels (MUST/SHOULD), and rationale grounding in validated EndUser pain points and confirmations.

Eight prioritized user requirements synthesized from interview records, enduser pain points, and confirmations. MUST-level requirements establish jerk minimization (≤0.5 m/s³), hard curvature constraints (vehicle-specific κ limits), iterative QP for non-convex obstacles (100–200 ms convergence, 5–10% suboptimality), and absolute SafetyAgent priority in safety-critical scenarios. SHOULD-level requirements address explicit mode-switching logic and curvature relaxation boundaries. COULD-level requirement covers real-time QP monitoring fallbacks. All items traced to ISO/IEC/IEEE 29148 and BABOK v3 practices.

Targeted deployer dialogue probing infrastructure capacity (hardware, real-time guarantees, fallback mechanisms), security/safety certification requirements (ISO 26262, SOTIF, mode-switching constraints), fleet scalability (vehicle-specific parameter management), production observability (telemetry, convergence validation), safety-critical validation gates (SafetyAgent priority enforcement testing), and non-convex obstacle handling latency budgets to ensure the trajectory planning system's jerk minimization, curvature constraints, and iterative QP approach are operationally viable at scale.

Deployer-focused dialogue probing infrastructure readiness (compute platforms, real-time guarantees, sensor fusion), safety certification alignment (ASIL, ODD, functional safety standards), fleet heterogeneity (multi-vehicle curvature calibration), network resilience (V2X latency degradation), and operational validation (comfort measurement, rollover margin validation, mode transition timing). These questions bridge the gap between the confirmed safety-efficiency trade-off requirements and practical deployment constraints.

Chain-of-Thought reasoning: The conflict scenario between SafetyAgent (passive safety, hard constraints) and EfficiencyAgent (smoothness, jerk <0.5 m/s³) is clarified in enduser confirmations but requires deployer input on infrastructure, real-time guarantees, safety certification, and integration touchpoints. Targeted questions probe: (1) compute platform constraints affecting QP convergence timing, (2) multi-vehicle scalability and ODD compliance, (3) hard vs. soft real-time feasibility, (4) sensor/MRM integration readiness, and (5) production monitoring for suboptimality validation. These probe infrastructure constraints (compute, latency), security mandates (functional safety, ODD), and scalability expectations (obstacle density, vehicle platforms) per the Interviewer role directive.

Infrastructure and operational framework for autonomous vehicle trajectory planning with SafetyAgent-EfficiencyAgent conflict resolution: edge compute with 200+ TFLOPS GPU capacity, deterministic RTOS for <50 ms latency, cryptographic validation of QP inputs, explicit mode-switching state machine prioritizing safety over comfort, QP convergence within 100–200 ms with 5–10% suboptimality fallback, vehicle-specific curvature calibration, and telemetry-driven passenger comfort monitoring. Scalability targets support 5–50 vehicle fleets with centralized obstacle synchronization.

These queries bridge operational context gaps between safety-efficiency conflict resolution (confirmed by end-user) and infrastructure deployment constraints (RTOS, edge compute, security mandates), ensuring feasibility before SRS formalization.

Deployer raises 5 critical clarifications on compute budget allocation (GPU FLOPS vs. cryptographic overhead), real-time determinism under data-dependent QP convergence, cryptographic validation latency integration, multi-core scaling strategy, and SafetyAgent→EfficiencyAgent mode-switching execution. All clarifications are grounded in conflict between infrastructure constraints (IC-AD-001/004) and operational requirements (jerk minimization, QP convergence, security validation) requiring explicit timing and fallback specifications.

Deployer role identifies four critical operational context gaps requiring stakeholder clarification: (1) compute budget allocation across QP solving, cryptographic validation, and sensor fusion within 200 TFLOPS constraint; (2) reconciliation of fixed <5ms jitter requirement with data-dependent iterative QP convergence variability; (3) cryptographic validation latency integration and bypass logic for real-time safety scenarios; (4) compute resource partitioning and priority scheduling between SafetyAgent and EfficiencyAgent during mode transitions. All clarifications are grounded in ISO/IEC/IEEE 29148 deployment environment checklist and infrastructure-security-scalability trade-off analysis.

Deployment requirements VALIDATED for infrastructure (200 TFLOPS edge compute, QNX/ROS2-DDS RTOS), security (cryptographic validation on separate core <10ms overhead), and scalability (8-core multi-threaded QP solver). SafetyAgent priority conflict RESOLVED via preemptible task scheduling with hard real-time interrupt. Curvature constraints confirmed as non-negotiable hard limits integrated into QP formulation. Outstanding: confirm cryptographic validation architecture and latency budget to finalize compute allocation and jitter guarantees.

Deployer validates feasibility of jerk minimization <0.5 m/s³ with iterative QP on edge compute (NVIDIA Drive Orin, 200 TFLOPS) within 100-200ms cycles. Curvature constraints (κ_max = 0.15 m⁻¹) are non-negotiable hard limits; SafetyAgent has absolute priority in MRM scenarios with <5ms interrupt latency on QNX Neutrino RTOS. Cryptographic SHA-256 validation (3ms overhead) executes in parallel preprocessing pipeline outside critical path. Multi-core architecture (8+ cores) isolates validation, QP solver, and safety threads for deterministic real-time scheduling. 5-10% QP suboptimality threshold maintains cost-performance trade-off without over-provisioning. One clarification pending: finalize cryptographic latency budget as percentage of planning cycle and confirm worst-case QP convergence includes simultaneous MRM trigger scenarios.

Deployment requirements validated for edge compute (NVIDIA Drive Orin, 200+ TFLOPS) with jerk minimization <0.5 m/s³ achievable within 100-200ms planning cycles. SafetyAgent interrupt priority <5ms enforced via QNX RTOS preemption. Curvature constraints (κ_max = 0.15 m⁻¹) are hard non-negotiable limits in QP formulation. Cryptographic validation (2-3ms) isolated to dedicated processor. Scalability via 8-core multi-tasking with fallback geometric planner. Real-time determinism guaranteed through explicit mode transitions and safety-critical latency bounds.

Comprehensive operating environment specification for AD trajectory planning system: NVIDIA Drive Orin/Snapdragon Ride (200+ TFLOPS GPU), 8-core CPU with 16GB RAM, QNX Neutrino RTOS with <5ms jitter guarantee, SHA-256 cryptographic validation pipeline, hard real-time scheduling for 100-200ms iterative QP cycles, ASIL B functional safety compliance, sensor synchronization <10ms latency, and thermal/power management for sustained autonomous vehicle operation. Environment enforces constraint-hierarchical execution where curvature limits are non-negotiable hard constraints, SafetyAgent interrupt latency <5ms, and jerk minimization operates within feasible solution space.
